name: Security Engineering
guide:
Security Engineering, as we track it, is the discipline that builds and operates the tools and infrastructure the rest of a security organization relies on. Day to day, a security engineer designs identity and access systems, builds detection content for a SIEM or EDR platform, hardens networks, and automates the guardrails that keep other teams from having to think about security manually. This is different from Application and Product Security, where the engineer sits inside a product team and reviews code, runs static and dynamic analysis, and threat-models a specific feature before it ships. Security Engineering tends to work at the platform level, building the systems that many product teams then plug into, rather than reviewing any one codebase line by line.

The line between Security Engineering and Cloud and Infrastructure Security is thinner, and the two overlap constantly in our data. Cloud and Infrastructure Security is scoped to hardening the environments themselves, meaning AWS, Azure, or GCP account structure, network segmentation, and workload configuration. Security Engineering more often owns the tooling layer that sits on top, things like the detection pipeline, identity provider, and vulnerability management program, and can span on-premises and cloud alike. Offensive Security is the opposite motion entirely, since a red team or penetration tester finds the gaps by attacking systems, while Security Engineering builds the defenses those attackers are testing.

Detection and Incident Response owns the pager, the alert queue, and the actual response to a live incident, while Security Engineering builds the detection engineering content and tooling the response team then operates day to day. Security Governance, Risk, and Compliance owns the audits, the policy language, and frameworks like ISO 27001, SOC 2, and FedRAMP, while a security engineer implements the technical controls those frameworks require without owning the compliance narrative itself. Security Leadership sits above all of these as management, budget, and strategy work, distinct from the individual-contributor and technical-lead work most Security Engineering postings describe.

On credentials, a computer science or related technical degree appears often in our postings but reads as one path among several rather than a strict requirement, especially for candidates who can show hands-on systems or networking experience. Classic industry certifications like CISSP, CISA, OSCP, CISM, and the GIAC or SANS lineup do not show up as tagged requirements in our current Security Engineering postings, so we cannot say employers here are asking for them by name. What does show up repeatedly are cloud-specific security certifications, with AWS security credentials appearing in 101 postings and Azure security credentials in 38, tracking with how much of this work now happens on cloud platforms. Treat those cloud certs as genuinely useful signal for this discipline, and treat the broader industry certification names as decorative until our own data shows otherwise.

Experience requirements in our sample skew toward the middle of the career ladder, with mid-level postings far outnumbering junior or intern listings, and a meaningful tail of senior, lead, principal, and director-level roles above that. Early-career hires tend to get in through internships, help desk or IT operations backgrounds, or junior analyst roles rather than a straight line into security engineering. What gets someone hired at the mid and senior level is demonstrated hands-on work, building or operating identity systems, detection tooling, or cloud security controls, more than credentials alone.

The technical skills our postings ask for most often include NIST framework knowledge, incident response, vulnerability management, SIEM platforms, and endpoint detection and response tooling, alongside AWS, Azure, and GCP experience and infrastructure tools like Kubernetes and Terraform. Python, Rust, Scala, and Java appear as the programming languages tied to this work, reflecting how much of modern security engineering now involves building tooling and automation rather than only configuring vendor products. Application security, threat modeling, identity and access management, zero trust architecture, and cryptography round out the more specialized end of the skill list.

Right now we currently track approximately 434 open postings in this category. Across the 2,044 of those postings in our broader sample that include salary figures, the average listed range runs from about $118,359 to $135,504 per year, with senior, staff, and principal roles pushing well above that band and entry-level roles well below it. The companies posting most often in this category include SimVentions, NTT DATA, Elastic, Leidos, the Defense Information Systems Agency, L3Harris Technologies, ServiceNow, MANTECH, Datadog, Anthropic, OpenAI, and J.P. Morgan, with a heavy concentration of government and defense contracting work alongside a growing cluster of postings from AI companies securing their own infrastructure.
